ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Endocrinology Consultation — Ann Richards — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Four-week bone health review with endocrinology consultation

text.paragraph: Low bone mass on DXA with a FRAX risk above the treatment thresholds in a 63-year-old woman after a fall with a hand fracture. Please confirm how to classify her, whether to treat and with what, and how to monitor. [S]

list.item: Is this osteoporosis or low bone mass, and should the hand fracture count as a fragility fracture in FRAX and in the diagnosis?
Is drug treatment indicated, and what is her risk category?
Which drug do you recommend for her, and what has to be in place before the first dose?
Is the secondary-causes work-up adequate?
How should we monitor her, when should DXA be repeated, and how long should treatment last before a drug holiday is considered?
Do her falls, her past smoking, or her alcohol use disorder in remission change the plan?

text.paragraph: Ms. Richards is seen at the request of Dr. Teague four weeks after her intake visit. She fell from standing height last year and broke her hand, and one account describes a second fall with an ankle fracture. She watched her mother live with fractures of the arm and hip and a curved back, and she wants to avoid that. She went through menopause in her early fifties and took no hormone therapy. She has never taken glucocorticoids or other drugs that harm bone. She smoked heavily for many years and stopped more than fifteen years ago, and she has not had alcohol for more than fifteen years. She walks and lifts weights, and since intake she has raised her calcium intake to about 1200 mg a day from food and taken vitamin D3 1971 units daily. She has no bone pain, kidney stones, or bowel symptoms. She travels most weeks for work and would like a treatment she does not have to remember daily. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Ann Richards was born Dorothy Ann Willis on September 1, 1933, in Lakeview, near Waco, Texas. [D]

She was elected Texas state treasurer in 1982, gave the keynote address at the 1988 Democratic National Convention, was elected governor of Texas in 1990, and served one term after losing her bid for re-election in 1994. [D]

She spoke openly about her past heavy drinking ("I smoked like a chimney and drank like a fish"), entered treatment, and emerged sober; one biography dates the treatment to 1980 and describes it as successful. [D]
She said publicly that her mother had osteoporosis, broke "her arm, her hip," and developed a hump, and that osteoporosis was not the cause of her mother's death but led to it. [D]
Because of her mother's fractures, she asked her doctor at an annual checkup to test her bone density. [D]

She had a bone density test after falling and breaking her hand. CBS News (2003) and a publisher's summary date this to 1996, and CBS says she fell twice and broke her hand and her ankle; a Publishers Weekly review dates the hand fracture to 1994. [D]
The bone density test showed osteopenia, which CBS News and the publisher's summary call an early stage of osteoporosis; in other interviews she said she had osteoporosis or early osteoporosis. [D]

text.paragraph: 4 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.

text.paragraph: No results recorded at this visit.

list.item: Low bone mass with high fracture risk (M85.89). By T-score this is low bone mass, not osteoporosis: the lowest value is -2.3 at the lumbar spine, and none is -2.5 or lower. The phrase early osteoporosis has no defined meaning and should not be used. A hand fracture is not one of the fractures that establishes osteoporosis on its own (hip or vertebra, or in low bone mass a proximal humerus, pelvis, or distal forearm fracture), but it followed a fall from standing height, so it is correctly entered as a previous fracture in FRAX. With that and her mother's hip fracture, FRAX is 22 percent for a major osteoporotic fracture and 3.6 percent for hip fracture, above the thresholds of 20 and 3 percent. Treatment is indicated by the BHOF 1993 and Endocrine Society thresholds, and AACE 1991 would call this osteoporosis on clinical grounds. By AACE 1991 she is in the very-high-risk group because of a fall with injury and a fracture within about the past year; she does not meet the Endocrine Society very-high-risk criteria, which center on severe or multiple vertebral fractures. [S]

Drug choice. Zoledronic acid 5 mg once a year is a first-line choice in both the high-risk and very-high-risk groups of AACE 1991 and is an initial therapy in the Endocrine Society guideline, with proven reduction of hip, vertebral, and nonvertebral fractures. Once-yearly dosing suits her travel. Anabolic therapy was discussed; with no vertebral fracture and no T-score below -2.5 it is not needed first, and it remains the option if she fractures on treatment. An oral bisphosphonate is a reasonable alternative. A selective estrogen receptor modulator is not suitable, because it has not been shown to reduce hip fractures and her hip risk is above threshold. Before the first dose, 25-hydroxyvitamin D must be 30 ng/mL or more, calcium and eGFR must be normal (creatinine clearance 35 mL/min or more), and a routine dental examination should be done. [S]

Secondary causes. Normal calcium, PTH, phosphate, magnesium, alkaline phosphatase, kidney function, TSH, and blood count make hyperparathyroidism, osteomalacia, thyroid excess, and myeloma unlikely. Vitamin D of 24 ng/mL is insufficient and is being corrected. The 24-hour urine calcium is still needed to exclude hypercalciuria before treatment. Celiac serology and protein electrophoresis are not needed without bowel symptoms, anemia, or an unexplained abnormal result. [S]

Falls (Z91.81). Falls cause most of her fracture risk outside the spine. Her tandem stance of 8 seconds shows impaired balance; a supervised balance and strength program is the most effective fall-prevention step. [S]

Alcohol use disorder in sustained remission (F10.21). Heavy alcohol use and smoking harm bone; her long abstinence from both removes them as current risk factors, so neither is entered as current in FRAX. Remission also lowers her fall risk. No change to the drug plan; avoid sedating medicines. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Intake DXA of the spine and hip, the lateral spine vertebral fracture assessment, the FRAX calculation and its inputs, the secondary-causes tests, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, fasting CTX, the three-day food record, and the intake fall-risk assessment. The 24-hour urine calcium has not yet been collected. [S]

list.item: Treat: zoledronic acid 5 mg intravenously once a year, starting once 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 30 ng/mL or more, calcium and eGFR are normal, and a routine dental examination is done; recheck these at about three months. [S]
Collect the 24-hour urine calcium before the first dose. [S]
Acetaminophen for the aches and fever that can follow the first dose. [S]
Continue vitamin D3 1971 units daily and about 1200 mg of calcium a day, mostly from food. [S]
Supervised balance and strength program now, then a home program; weight-bearing exercise most days. [S]
Fasting morning CTX three months after the first dose to confirm response; calcium and creatinine before each yearly dose; 25-hydroxyvitamin D yearly. [S]
Repeat DXA of the spine and hip two years after starting, on the same scanner. [S]

After three yearly doses, recalculate FRAX and reassess: a drug holiday of up to three years is reasonable if she has had no new fracture or injurious fall and the femoral neck T-score is above -2.5; if she remains at very high risk, continue to six yearly doses. [S]
Height and fall-risk screen yearly, with repeat vertebral imaging if height falls 2 cm or more. [S]
Discussed with Dr. Teague the same day; the patient agrees with the plan and asked for once-yearly treatment. [S]

Follow-up: Primary care will continue monitoring on the CMID osteoporosis schedule. Endocrinology will see her again for a fracture on treatment, a fall in bone density on the follow-up DXA, an abnormal secondary-causes result, or the drug-holiday decision after the third dose. [S]
